newsitem.title: GERMANY: German tax revenues seen falling billions short.
newsitem.headline: German tax revenues seen falling billions short.

text.p: The German government's autumn estimate of tax revenues due on Friday is expected to show that inflows will be billions of marks short of previous projections, analysts said on Thursday.

Sources in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition estimated federal tax revenues at two billion marks ($1.3 billion) to three billion marks less than the last estimate in May. State and local governments and other public institutions would add billions more to the total.
The Bonn government is already locked in a bitter dispute about cutting state spending to meet the strict criteria for the single European currency during 1997.
Further shortfalls in the tax revenue estimate, which all parties accept as the benchmark for their budget calculations, will only step up the pressure for more politically sensitive spending cuts.
"Tax revenues for 1996 and 1997 have already been sharply reduced in the past two estimates," said Joachim Poss, financial spokesman for the opposition Social Democrats (SPD).
The government needs to boost revenue to meet its obligations, he said, but "the opposite will be the case" when Friday's tax estimate comes out.

The keenly awaited estimate is drawn up twice a year by a panel of economists from the federal and state governments, the Bundesbank and private research institutes and is widely seen as a nonpartisan benchmark for fiscal policy.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Thursday estimated the federal government's 1997 spending gap at three billion marks, and said he could cover one billion marks through cuts in social spending.
Economist Holger Fahrinkrug at UBS in Frankfurt estimated taxes would be five billion marks less than the May forecast. "A double-digit number would clearly be a very bad surprise," he said.

Economic sluggishness -- particularly in the first quarter of this year -- as well as continued high unemployment and loopholes are seen as the main factors depressing tax revenue. The rebound now under way is not brightening the picture yet.

"Tax revenues are no longer responding as much to economic growth as in the past. Germans are getting ever better at responding to tax breaks," said economist Holger Schmieding at Merrill Lynch in Frankfurt.
In east Germany, people are rushing to exploit a whopping 50 percent depreciation allowance for housing and other construction projects that expires this year, Schmieding said.

The overall federal deficit is now expected to total 56.5 billion marks in 1997, but many economists are sceptical this target will be met. Waigel has failed to restrain the 1996 deficit at 60 billion marks and it is now seen ballooning to 70 billion marks.
Waigel, who originally wanted the 1997 deficit to be only 2.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), has had to admit it may now end up around the three percent target the Maastricht Treaty sets.
For 1996, it is nearing 4.0 percent of GDP.
The May estimate of tax revenues projected 1997 federal tax revenues at 349.1 billion marks, up from 340.1 billion marks this year.
Total public sector tax revenues were seen at 841.2 billion marks, up from 807.1 billion marks.
